<reason>The debate reduced to one question: what counts as "traditional expectations" — A's pedigree test (old, cross-cultural, enacting vs. displaying) or B's lived test (whatever is enforced under tradition's name). A controlled that clash from the opening and won it. A's Q2 exposed that B's opening debunked the diamond as "recent marketing" using a pedigree intuition, but when pressed in B4.2, B disclaimed pedigree entirely; A's R2 and closing showed the replacement criterion was circular (the motion becomes "owe little to whatever people pressure you to do"), inconsistent with B1.5, and over-inclusive. B fought back hard: the fork in B2.7–B2.8 and the "proposition in CON's own voice" turn were genuinely damaging, and B's framing fit the motion's evident intent better. But those moves only bite if B's definitional ruling is accepted, and that ruling was the part of B's case that degraded under pressure. A's parasite/host spine stayed consistent across all five speeches, B's concessions on witnesses and chosen community were cleanly converted, and both sides were impeccably disciplined — no fake sourcing, clean Q1/Q2 and A1/A2 execution. Razor-thin, but A made the decisive clash clearer and left B's route to victory resting on a criterion B itself destabilized.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's pressure question Q2 (what criterion separates the "marketing" diamond from the "traditional" guest list) forced B to abandon pedigree in B4.2, which A4.3–A4.4 and A5.2 then converted into a triple charge — circularity, self-contradiction, proving too much — that B never repaired.</best_rebuttal>
